newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysian shares plunge, break key barriers.
newsitem.headline: Malaysian shares plunge, break key barriers.

text.p: Malaysian shares rode a smooth downward slide on Tuesday, with the key blue-chip index plummeting more than 3.4 percent after breaking the 950-point support level.
Analysts and brokers said the stock market was reacting to a string of announcements perceived as negative for the economy.

The bearish tone was exacerbated by news late on Monday of a huge trade deficit in June and the central bank's announcement on Sunday that it was imposing curbs on currency swaps done by local banks, the brokers and analysts said.

At the close on Tuesday, the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange Composite Index was down 3.42 percent, or 33.48 points, to 945.08. Earlier, it had plunged to 944.51, a new 1997 low. The index has lost nearly 6.2 percent in two days.
Brokers and analysts said many foreign funds relentlessly sold down key index-weighted stocks.
The sell-off in Malaysia was echoed in Thailand, where stocks fell 2.31 percent. Singapore foreign tranche shares were also down and the Indonesian market was weak near its close.
Among the most active stocks in Malaysia were large-capitalised issues such as Telekom, Maybank and Tenaga, which fell between 30 cents and 1.10 ringgit.

"The rumour is that a (U.S. financier George) Soros fund has sold 1,000 lots (of 200 shares each) of Maybank through Singapore. I have confirmed this with two independent parties," said a dealing manager at a local brokerage house.
Soros has been named by Malaysian Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad as responsible for causing havoc in Southeast Asian currencies over the past two months.
"There is only bad news in a market already weak on sentiment," said an analyst with a bank-backed brokerage.
Malaysia announced a 2.8 billion ringgit trade deficit in June, the biggest monthly deficit in 17 years, analysts said.

On Sunday, the central Bank Negara Malaysia announced a limit of $2.0 million on local banks' currency swap exposure to any one overseas customer, a move seen by analysts as regressive for the fast-growing and liberalising Malaysia.
"I think what is happening is a stroke of bad luck for the central bank," said Lum Chee Soon, general manager of economic research at Phileo Allied Securities in Kuala Lumpur.
He said the introduction of restrictions on swaps was inconsistent with Malaysia's policy of a freely floating currency. "It sends the wrong signals to the market."
"Bank Negara should be more focused in their policy," Lum said.
"In the last few days, people are just scrambling to get out. And it is mostly foreign investors," he said.
Some analysts said there was talk the Composite Index could head as low as 850, blaming the possibility entirely on the new capital control measures of Bank Negara.

"The fall (in share prices) is more to do with Bank Negara's measures than the trade data. People are saying that they don't have a game plan and are making ad hoc moves," said the chief investment officer with a Malaysian fund management firm.
"There are short players looking to roll over their ringgit positions, but now they are being forced to sell shares. They are scrambling to raise ringgit.
"I am sitting in a state of shock here. There are tonnes of cheap stocks out there, but people are too scared," he said.

Malaysian stock prices have been in the doldrums since late March, when the central Bank Negara announced curbs on banks' lending to the property sector and for share purchases. The blue-chip index has lost 22 percent since March 28 and more than 25 percent since its peak of 1,278.94 on February 26.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-201 4813)
